```
        if messages is None:
```

Why we can delete this: 
The two lines deleted is in every `generate_<>_reply` function. So when both messages and sender are passed to a subsequent `generate_<>_reply`, it will perform the same logic.
```
final, reply = reply_func(self, messages=messages, sender=sender, config=reply_func_tuple["config"])
```

body: Great question! Empirically, it worked better on my tests than giving the instructions only once, whether before or after the text. And conceptually, this is what I expected would happen. The instructions often (but not always) consist of two parts: the description of the analysis, followed by the required format of the response. If the text appears first in the message, then the vector columns that process the text know nothing about the analysis to be performed. But if the analysis tokens come first, then the text vector columns are conditioned directly on the analysis tokens and vector columns, which seems like a more efficient use of transformer computation. But there are also benefits to having the analysis tokens appear for a second time at the end. They give the LLM more tokens to reason over, and force it to revisit the instructions. This is most useful as the text to be analyzed grows in length. Finally, it's important to have any output format requirements at the very end, so they don't get ignored.

OK, please see a revised section of "Static and dynamic conversations". I had to rewrite the section so that it flows coherently from point to point. Hope it's ok.

#### Static and dynamic conversations

AutoGen, by integrating conversation-driven control utilizing both programming and natural language, inherently supports dynamic conversations. This dynamic nature allows the agent topology to adapt based on the actual conversation flow under varying input problem scenarios. Conversely, static conversations adhere to a predefined topology. Dynamic conversations are particularly beneficial in complex settings where interaction patterns cannot be predetermined.

1. Dynamic Group Chat
The system enables dynamic group chat through a registered auto-reply function. This function allows initiating conversations with other agents based on the current message and context. A practical example is demonstrated in [dynamic group chat](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/blob/main/notebook/agentchat_groupchat.ipynb) which illustrates the management of dynamic group chats and the decision process for the next speaker.

2. Graph-Based Group Chat
In this approach, a directed graph is fed into [GraphGroupChat](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/blob/main/notebook/agentchat_two_users.ipynb), an inherited class of `GroupChat`. AutoGen then performs several functions: (1) It seeks a speaker suggestion from the previous speaker, thereby reducing API calls. (2) In the absence of a suggestion, it utilizes the LLM API to nominate the next speaker amongst the eligible speakers. (3) Lastly, it randomly selects from eligible speakers, defined as successor nodes (agents) from the prior speaker (agent). Note that for simpler use cases where all nodes are interconnected, `GroupChat` suffices. However, `GraphGroupChat` is useful for more controlled scenarios requiring specific conversation paths.

3. LLM-Based Function Call
Another approach involves LLM-based function calls, where LLM decides if a specific function should be invoked based on the conversation's status during each inference. This approach enables dynamic multi-agent conversations, as seen in scenarios like [multi-user math problem solving scenario](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/blob/main/notebook/agentchat_two_users.ipynb), where a student assistant automatically seeks expertise via function calls.

body:
Hey @sonichi, before I work on the code, can we expand on this point?

1. `allow_repeat_speaker` is currently used as a check against `speaker_order_dict`, without favoring either parameter.
1a. If `allow_repeat_speaker` is True, then, self-loops are allowed in `speaker_order_dict` for any agent.  We do not create any self-loops in `speaker_order_dict`, just validation checks.
1b. If `allow_repeat_speaker` is a list of Agents, then, self-loops are allowed only for the named agents in `speaker_order_dict`. We do not create/delete any self-loops in `speaker_order_dict`, just validation checks.
1c. If `allow_repeat_speaker` is set to False, then, no self-loops are allowed in `speaker_order_dict` for all agents. Similarly, we do not delete any self-loops present in `speaker_order_dict` but simply raise an error.
1d. These validations are done in `graph_utils.check_graph_validity`. 

2. I would recommend for `allow_repeat_speaker` **not** to be ignored because I think that favoring one parameter as ground-truth (`speaker_order_dict`) and ignoring another parameter (`allow_repeat_speaker`) when both are supplied causes silent failures/ surprises to the user. Extending this principle, I would also not recommend favoring `allow_repeat_speaker` over `speaker_order_dict` by editing `speaker_order_dict` to fit `allow_repeat_speaker`.
2a. FYI `allow_repeat_speaker` is currently defaulted to True in the initialization of `GroupChat`. `allow_repeat_speaker: Optional[Union[bool, List[Agent]]] = True`. I am not sure of the impact of setting `allow_repeat_speaker` to None for now. 
4. I think you are refering to L86-90 of `groupchat.py` instead of `graph_utils.py`. L86-90 is to create the `allowed_speaker_order` so that the rest of the code work with the **whitelist**. I am assuming that all allowed or disallowed self-loops are supplied in `allowed_or_disallowed_speaker_order` (old name `speaker_order_dict`) by the user, and therefore, not considering `allow_repeat_speaker` in L86-90 and only consider it in L93 where `graph_utils.check_graph_validity` is called.

Curious to hear your thoughts on whether any changes is required. :)
